  MINUTES
  Regular Meeting
  ALHAMBRA CITY COUNCIL
  Ruth Reese Hall, 101 South First Street
  March 8, 2021
  6:00 p.m.

ROLL CALL: At 6:03 p.m., on Monday, March 8, 2021 the Alhambra City Council met via video
conference.

COUNCIL PRESENT via video conference: LEE, MAZA, MALONEY, ANDRADE-STADLER,
PÉREZ
ABSENT:  NONE

Officials Present physically, via teleconference, and via video conference: City Manager
Binnquist, City Attorney Montes, Assistant City Manager Garcia, Deputy City Manager Tran,
City Clerk Myles, Director of Finance Lieu, Director of Public Works/ Utilities Ray, Director of
Parks and Recreation Macias, Marketing and Communications Specialist Nguyen, Management
Analyst Cuevas, Director of Community Development Castagnola, Fire Chief Phelps, Police
Chief Vu, Director of Human Resources Ko

FLAG SALUTE:  Mayor Pérez

CITY CLERK REPORT - NOTICE NO. N2M21-26

The City Clerk reported that she duly gave notice of the regular meeting of the City Council
being held pursuant to the order of the Mayor in accordance with Section 54955 and 54956 of
the Government Code of the State of California.

CEREMONIAL

1.  COMMENDATION: ALHAMBRA HOSPITAL MEDICAL CENTER – F2M21-3

  Mayor Pérez and the Alhambra City Council, on behalf of the citizens of Alhambra
  wished to commend and thank Alhambra Hospital Medical Center for their partnership,
  hard work and collaboration in the fast, efficient and safe administration of the COVID-19
  vaccine to Alhambra Fire, Police and other essential City personnel. The City of
  Alhambra deeply appreciated the extraordinary efforts of the Alhambra Hospital Medical
  Center Management and Staff who ensured essential city personnel were provided
  protection against the COVID-19 virus. The City of Alhambra was grateful for the
  Alhambra Hospital Medical Center’s continuous efforts to promote the health and well-
  being of their patients and our community. A commendation was presented to Alhambra
  Hospital Medical Center.

2.  PROCLAMATION AGAINST HATE ACTS RELATED TO COVID-19 – F2M21-3
  1
3-8-21
   Ratified the action of Mayor Pérez in proclaiming that the City Council would continue its
  efforts to protect all residents who are targets of hate and to curb hate acts related to
  COVID-19 and that the City Council urged Alhambra residents to join the Council in
  calling attention to the harms of discrimination and aggression against specific
  communities, including Asian American Pacific Islanders, and denounced hate to help
  keep us all safe during the unprecedented pandemic and beyond.

PRESENTATIONS

3.  RESULTS OF COMMUNITY SATISFACTION SURVEY – F2M18-35

  Assistant City Manager GARCIA delivered a staff report and introduced Dr. Timothy
  MCLARNEY, president of True North Research. On December 14, 2020, based on Goal
  14 of the Alhambra 2020-21 Strategic Plan, the City Council directed staff move forward
  with engaging a professional consultant to conduct a Community Satisfaction Survey.
  The purpose of the Community Satisfaction Survey was to obtain statistically reliable
  data to improve the City’s understanding of the residents’ satisfaction, priorities, and
  concerns as they related to services, facilities, and policies provided by the City. The
  data provided important support to the City as new strategic or budget decisions were
  considered. The City engaged True North Research to design the research plan and
  conduct the survey. True North was a full-service survey research firm dedicated to
  providing agencies with understanding of community perceptions, concerns, and
  priorities. The firm had conducted over 1,000 survey research studies for more than 400
  cities and school districts. Alhambra’s Community Satisfaction Survey was broadly
  defined and designed to help identify: key resident issues; satisfaction with City services;
  opinions on strategic topics; satisfaction with communications and engagement; and
  other background and demographic data to understand needs, perceptions, and
  interests. Mr. MCLARNEY from True North Research delivered a PowerPoint
  presentation to the City Council details regarding the results of the Community
  Satisfaction Survey, which is on file in the City Clerk’s office. The fully detailed results of
  the survey were featured in the final report prepared by True North and it was available
  on the City’s website at https://www.cityofalhambra.org/resources/public-outreach and is
  on file in the City Clerk’s office.

  Discussion: Council thanked Mr. McLarney for the detailed report and expressed
  encouragement at the positive responses to the survey. Council expressed appreciation
  for city staff and that the positive responses were reflections of their hard work.
  Councilmember MALONEY and Mr. MCLARNEY discussed the survey methods used by
  other cities. Councilmember ANDRADE-STADLER and Mr. MCLARNEY discussed the
  ways in which the COVID-19 pandemic affected resident responses and the more open
  availability of residents. Councilmember LEE discussed the participation distribution
  across Alhambra with Mr. MCLARNEY. Ms. LEE and Mayor PÉREZ commented on the
  usefulness of the survey results during their townhall meetings to help direct discussion.
  Ms. PÉREZ stated that many of the highlighted items reflected items on the Strategic
  Plan.

  Action Taken:  City Council received and filed the 2021 Community Satisfaction
  Survey.

  2
3-8-21
 4.  NEEDS ASSESSMENT, FEASIBILITY STUDY, PROGRAMMING AND CONCEPT
  FOR THE REHABILITATION OF THE SHORB CLINIC PROPERTY INTO A
  COMMUNITY CENTER – F2M18-54

  Community Development Director CASTAGNOLA delivered a staff report and introduced
  Linda CHEU, Lucia FISCHER, and Bob COFFEE from AECOM who delivered a
  PowerPoint presentation, all of which are on file in the City Clerk’s office. In April 2019,
  the City Council deliberated the Strategic Plan Objectives for fiscal year 2019-20 and
  adopted Goal No. 5 to develop a plan for the rehabilitation of the Shorb Clinic into a
  Community Center, and in May 2019, the Los Angeles County Board of Supervisors
  approved a return of the property to the City of Alhambra. On October 28, 2019, the City
  Council retained AECOM to evaluate community center programmatic needs, assess the
  existing building conditions, and develop and analyze alternatives for community center
  development. The AECOM team included engineers, architects, estimators and
  financing advisors. The study progressed, amid the pandemic, over the course of 14
  months and included the following tasks: review of population and demographic trends
  for Alhambra and surrounding area; evaluation of current and past recreation
  programming levels and participation information; examination of key characteristics of
  existing Alhambra facilities; interviews with key stakeholders, including Parks &
  Recreation staff, instructors and City officials; conducted a community needs survey;
  performed on-site assessment of existing structure conditions; developed a proposed
  building program based on community input. The AECOM representatives presented the
  three illustrative building concepts developed and corresponding cost estimates as
  follows: Scheme 1: Partial Building Reuse; Scheme 2: New Construction within the
  bounds of the existing parcel; and, Scheme 3: New Construction with closure of Shorb
  Street between 6th and 7th Streets. Based on the consultant’s conclusion to adopt
  Scheme 3 as the preferred conceptual design to best meet the community’s needs, staff
  sought direction from the City Council to pursue this or another alternative for further
  design refinement.

  Public Comment:  Joyce AMARO spoke in favor of the community center, but
  advocated for preservation of the building due to its historic nature and possible
  designation as an historic place on the National Register of Historic Places.

  Public Comment received via email on file in the City Clerk’s office:

  The following people wrote in favor of Scheme 1: Partial Building Reuse:

  1) Jeanne Carter
  2) Dr. Yelba Maria Carrillo
  3) Susan Bejeckian
  4) Kim Cooper and Richard Schave
  5) Elizabeth Salinas
  6) Liz Demus
  7) James Demus
  8) Nicholas Cobian
  9) Melissa Michelson
  10) Erika Cobian
  11) Daryl Chou
  3
3-8-21
   12) Efren Moreno Jr.
  13) Oscar Amaro, representing the Alhambra Preservation Group
  14) William and Gisela Adams
  15) Lois Wadsworth
  16) Chris Olson
  17) Meehar Tom
  18) Linda Trevillian
  19) Isolda Robinson
  20) Michael Lawrence

  Additional Public Comment:

  1) Shirley TATSUNO wrote in support of the community center and option 3. She went
  on to support the development of Moor Field as an adjacent amenity in the future,
  the inclusion of affordable housing on the upper floors of the building, and that
  affordable senior classes be offered through the community center.

  2) Cliff BENDER wrote to question AECOM’s proposal which expanded the original
  request for a community center with open use to include more recreational activities
  offered through the Parks and Recreation department. He also supported full
  rehabilitation of the building rather than the proposed partial rehabilitation.

  Discussion: Councilmember MAZA suggested exploring additional options to preserve
  and use as much of the existing structure and encouraged the consultant to review the
  preservation work at the Iona Work Spaces project on Alhambra Road for inspiration. He
  acknowledged the difficulties in the property and expressed concerns regarding the
  costly remediation of the asbestos in the building. He suggested reviewing a
  combination of options and also supported closing Shorb Street and utilizing the street
  up to Moor Field. He encouraged staff seeking additional grant funding.

  Councilmember LEE expressed her preference to preserve the exterior of the building
  and to redesign the interior to become a multi-purpose building. She stressed the need
  to retrofit the building so that it was safe and reviewed the costs associated with each
  option. She discussed the specifics of Alternative 1 with Mr. COFFEE and Ms. CHEU.
  Ms. LEE reiterated her preference to preserve the exterior of the building and use Option
  1.

  Mr. COFFEE discussed their assessment of the existing structure and stated that it was
  incompatible with the program directive to use the building as a community center. He
  stated that given the existing building design, it was better suited to converting it into a
  school or housing. He stated that as a brick building, the Shorb Clinic was architecturally
  significant. But he continued to reiterate the difficulty in aligning the goals of preserving
  the existing building and converting it to a community center space. He encouraged
  Council to review other needs in the community, expressed sympathy for the speakers
  with emotional attachment to the building as well as the strong public desire for a
  community center, but stated that this was a more complex design prospect.

  Ms. LEE respected Mr. Coffee’s professional assessment and agreed with the
  constraints. She acknowledged the challenge to modernize the interior to conform to a
  new purpose while preserving the exterior. She restated her priority to preserve the
  4
3-8-21
   historically significant building and spoke to the benefits of older brick buildings. Mr.
  COFFEE stated that it was technically possible to preserve the brick façade, to
  modernize the electrical and plumbing, to add 1 or 2 additional parking spaces, but
  added that based on the public comment received there would have to be
  accommodations.

  Councilmember ANDRADE-STADLER discussed the background of the project, the
  history of the site, and the past discussions about retrofitting the property. She discussed
  Scheme 3 and the closure of Shorb Street and expressed preference for a combination
  of Scheme 1 to preserve the building and Scheme 3 which could incorporate an outdoor
  space. She referred to Mr. Maza’s suggestion to review the Iona Work Spaces. She
  requested that staff try to incorporate the outdoor space in a combination of Scheme 1
  and 3.

  Councilmember MALONEY stated that while he did not share the fond memories of the
  building expressed by others, that the building was significant for the community. He
  stated that the City would need to continue to explore different options and review the
  uses of the building. He supported the closure of Shorb Street in any scenario and
  partner with Alhambra Unified School District to make use of Moor Field. He reviewed
  the proposal for the multipurpose room on the grassy lawn or on Shorb Street instead of
  trying to fit it into the existing structure. He discussed removing the second story building
  and use that to include the multipurpose room and preserve the main building with Mr.
  COFFEE. He continued to review Council’s discussion and suggested that Council and
  staff continue to consider other options.

  Mayor PÉREZ thanked staff for their work on the project and expressed disappointment
  over absolute preservation of the entire building. She stated that based on the existing
  structure of the building’s interior, it would be an ideal fit for a housing development
  rather than a community center. She expressed concern over the time invested in
  exploring the community center program while preferring to preserve the building. She
  referred to other facilities with community centers and the features that comprise them.
  She also referred to the overall community support of an open space community center.
  She suggested pursuing Alternative 3 and bring in the design elements of Alternative 1.
  She stated that she could not see preserving the entire building while still making it a
  community center. She said if Council wanted to prioritize preserving the building, then it
  would be better to use it for housing. She stressed the need to consider both
  preferences of the community to preserve part of the building while providing all desired
  amenities of a community center. She stated that it would not be possible to include
  outdoor space while preserving the entire building and continued to refer to discussions
  with residents who expressed desire for more greenspace. She suggested that the
  history and design elements of the building could be expressed in other ways.

  Council, staff, and the consultants continued to discuss the direction of Council for
  AECOM to return with new options to preserve and incorporate as much of the existing
  building structure as possible while incorporating options for Shorb Street as
  greenspace.

  Ms. ANDRADE-STADLER suggested staff work with the Historic Preservation Society to
  further assess the property to fully address all concerns. Mr. CASTAGNOLA reviewed
  the current contract with the Historic Preservation Society and stated that the
  5
3-8-21
   assessment of a specific building would be a part of a later stage in the development of
  the Historic Preservation Ordinance. Ms. ANDRADE-STADLER suggested exploring
  grants to pay for the assessment by the Historic Preservation Group. Mr. MAZA
  supported Ms. Andrade-Stadler’s suggestion as a show of good faith to the community
  that all options were explored. He also suggested that AECOM could provide Council
  with a tour of the building to get a better perspective of the existing building. Ms. LEE
  continued to discuss the importance of preservation and seeking out grant funding. Ms.
  PÉREZ supported Mr. Maza’s suggestion of a tour of Shorb Clinic and requested that
  Council could tour one of AECOM’s recent projects. She also requested that staff
  explore options for using the building for a housing project. She went on to discuss the
  importance of outdoor spaces in light of the COVID-19 pandemic and any future
  pandemics. Ms. LEE supported exploring housing designs. Mr. MALONEY and Mr.
  MAZA supported continuing with designs for a community center with greenspace. Mr.
  Maza clarified that he would explore other program options once all other ideas have
  been exhausted for a community center.

  Ms. CHEU stated that they would review the scope of the existing contract with staff and
  review other cost options.

  Action Taken:  City Council received and ordered filed AECOM’s report for a
  needs assessment, feasibility study, programming and design concept options for the
  rehabilitation of the Shorb property and directed staff and AECOM to return with new
  options to preserve, provide new options to incorporate as much of the existing building
  structure as possible while incorporating options for Shorb Street as greenspace, and
  provide options for an alternate housing development.

5.  2020-2021 STRATEGIC PLAN UPDATE – F2M18-35

  Deputy City Manager TRAN delivered a staff report. On June 16, 2020, the City Council
  and executive staff held a strategic planning session to update the City’s Strategic Plan.
  The session involved discussion regarding priorities to be implemented into the City’s
  strategic plan. Approximately every year, the City Council and executive staff meet to
  revisit and/or update the priorities and set goals and objectives for the City accordingly.
  In addition, staff provides progress reports to the City Council on a quarterly basis. This
  was the final update to the current plan, and the Council’s next strategic planning
  session was set for March 11, 2021.

  Discussion: Councilmember MAZA thanked staff for their work, especially during the
  challenges of the COVID-19 pandemic. He highlighted the goal of acquiring a local hotel,
  related a potential project at West Valley Boulevard, and encouraged staff to look into
  the matter. Mayor PÉREZ thanked staff and expressed excitement for the next Planning
  Session.

  Action Taken:  City Council received and filed this informational report.

ANDRADE-STADLER:  Councilmember Andrade-Stadler left the meeting at approximately
9:21 p.m.

6.  REQUEST FOR SUPPORT FOR THE RESTORATION OF CONGRESSIONAL
  6
3-8-21
   EARMARKS FOR GROUNDWATER CLEANUP – F2M21-19, R2M21-16

  Deputy City Manager TRAN delivered a staff report. The Water Quality Authority (WQA)
  encouraged legislative actions for the reversal of federal legislation banning the use of
  limited Congressional earmarks. The WQA asked for the City’s support in reaching out
  to our local federal delegates for this purpose. The City of Alhambra agreed that
  obtaining federal earmarks would enhance the health of our region and benefit the City
  to advocate for such funding. In the past, federal earmarks have been used for a
  multitude of projects benefiting the region. These funds were vital to local efforts
  regarding groundwater cleanup projects, health care facilities, mental health programs
  and transportation projects. Specifically, earmarks were previously used in the City of
  Alhambra for groundwater cleanup.

ANDRADE-STADLER:  Councilmember Andrade-Stadler returned to the meeting via
audio only, at approximately 9:24 p.m.

  Discussion: Councilmember ANDRADE-STADLER discussed the reason behind the
  ban of the congressional earmarks in 2020 with Mr. Tran, City Manager BINNQUIST,
  and Councilmember MALONEY.

  Action Taken:  City Council adopted Resolution No. R2M21-16 entitled: A
  Resolution of the City Council of the City of Alhambra in support of the restoration of
  Congressional earmarks for groundwater cleanup, expressing the City of Alhambra’s
  support for the restoration of limited congressional earmarks and the accompanying
  letters that would be forwarded to our Senate and Congressional representatives for
  groundwater cleanup.

  Vote:  Moved:  ANDRADE-STADLER  Seconded:  LEE
  Ayes:  MAZA, MALONEY, ANDRADE-STADLER, LEE, PÉREZ
  Noes:  NONE
  Absent:  NONE

7.  DISCUSSION AND DIRECTION CONCERNING  POTENTIAL  OPT-IN  FOR
  DISPOSABLE UTENSILS ORDINANCE – F2M21-7

  City Attorney MONTES delivered a staff report. At the February 8, 2021 City Council
  meeting, Mayor Pérez requested, and the City Council consented to agendize, a
  discussion of potentially adopting an ordinance regulating the distribution of disposable
  utensils by food establishments in the City. If Council wished to adopt such an
  ordinance, City staff would require direction as to its scope (what would the ordinance
  apply to, and what restrictions specifically would be placed upon those items) and
  applicability (who/which businesses are subject to the ordinance). Additionally, staff
  required direction as to the extent of outreach, if any, the Council would like to see
  undertaken in connection with such effort.

  Discussion: Councilmember MALONEY supported the intention of the ordinance and
  that disposable utensils be provided upon request. He supported mirroring similar
  ordinances which were being drafted by the County as well as other local cities. He also
  supported reaching out to local restaurants for input.
  7
3-8-21
   Councilmember LEE discussed how the ordinance would affect restaurant delivery and
  the County’s provisions in their ordinance with Mr. MONTES. Ms. LEE discussed the
  challenges of the initial implementation of the ordinance, and suggested notifying the
  public by signs at the restaurant. She supported the ordinance as it might reduce costs
  for the restaurant.

  Mr. MONTES addressed Mr. Maloney’s suggestion to review similar ordinances by other
  cities, listed the differences between those proposed ordinances, and stated that staff
  could draft an ordinance with a more limited scope.

  Mayor PÉREZ expressed support of following the example of the County’s proposed
  ordinance. She reported on her discussion with representatives of the California
  Restaurants Association who supported the proposed ordinance and requested allowing
  an option for customers to request utensils and that the ordinance exclude self service
  dispensers or stations at restaurants. Mr. MONTES stated that staff could review the
  County’s draft ordinance when it was produced and would then present a draft to
  Council for discussion and approval.

ANDRADE-STADLER:  Councilmember  Andrade-Stadler  resumed  her  video  at
approximately 9:35 p.m.

  Councilmember MALONEY supported staff moving forward with drafting an ordinance
  for Council approval using the County’s model. Council agreed unanimously.

  Action Taken:  City Council directed staff to move forward with an ordinance draft
  for Council approval, using the County’s existing model, and to exclude self-service
  stands at restaurants from the ordinance.

8.  CONTINUED DISCUSSION CONCERNING COVID-19 HERO PAY FOR GROCERY
  RETAIL AND DRUG RETAIL WORKERS – F2M20-33

  City Attorney MONTES delivered a staff report. At the last few City Council meetings,
  Mayor Pérez requested, and the City Council consented to agendize, a discussion of
  potentially adopting a temporary “COVID-19 Hero Pay” ordinance requiring additional
  hourly pay for retail grocery and drug store workers. The discussion by the Council was
  postponed over a couple of meetings given the pending litigation over a similar
  ordinance adopted by the City of Long Beach. Additionally, the County of Los Angeles
  was scheduled to consider a similar ordinance, which might have applied to incorporated
  cities within the County. Since the last Alhambra City Council meeting, the County
  adopted an urgency ordinance temporarily requiring the payment of $5 per hour
  premium pay for grocery and drug retail employees within the unincorporated areas of
  the County. Additionally, a judge in the California Central District Federal court denied a
  request to enjoin enforcement of the Long Beach hero pay ordinance during the
  pendency of the litigation challenging the Long Beach ordinance.

  Public Comment:

  8
3-8-21
   1) Alice LU, an employee at Albertson’s grocery store, supported the ordinance and
  discussed her history with her company as well as the challenges and dangers faced
  by grocery workers during the pandemic.

  2) Rachel TORRES, representing the United Food and Commercial Workers, supported
  the ordinance and discussed the many cities which were considering or had
  implemented similar ordinances as well as the benefits to grocery workers.

  Public Comment received via email on file in the City Clerk’s office:

  The following people wrote against the ordinance:

  1)  Alex Perez
  2)  Philip Chen
  3)  J. Tran
  4)  David Mejia
  5)  William Yee

  Discussion: Councilmember ANDRADE-STADLER discussed the legal scope of the
  ordinance and mirroring the Long Beach ordinance for temporary pay increase, the
  sustainability of the cost for smaller grocery stores versus national chain stores,
  emphasized the temporary nature of the increased wages, and overall supported
  compensation for workers in light of the dangerous working conditions faced by workers
  during the height of the pandemic. She discussed the draft of the ordinance with Mr.
  MONTES. Mr. MONTES suggested that Council review the County’s proposed
  ordinance so that should Council decide to move forward, it would comply with the
  County ordinance. He went on to discuss the details of the County and Long Beach
  ordinances, and made recommendations as to which items the City could adopt for an
  ordinance.

  Councilmember MALONEY reported on the Federal Court ruling on the Long Beach
  ordinance, expressed concerns as to the City’s potential exposure to litigation, and
  offered support of the idea behind the ordinance. He recommended following the Long
  Beach model since it had been tested litigation already, and then adopting the
  improvements that were included in the County ordinance.

  Councilmember LEE supported the intent of the ordinance to provide workers with fair
  compensation and working conditions, reiterated her preference for this to have been
  settled by labor negotiations, and expressed her concerns with implementing the
  ordinance in Alhambra such as retaliation against employees and the City’s exposure to
  litigation. She continued to discuss the potential methods of retaliation such as employee
  transfers, increased use of self-checkout stands, cancelling other salary increases, or
  store closures. She continued to discuss other concerns with the long-term effects of the
  ordinance and opposed the ordinance.

  Councilmember MAZA echoed support of the intention behind the ordinance to support
  workers. He expressed concern as to the fairness of the ordinance in excluding other
  workers who have continued to work during the pandemic and continued to be exposed
  to the COVID-19 virus. He expressed that it was beyond the scope of the City Council to
  become involved in private enterprise and that this should be resolved by management
  9
3-8-21
   and workers. He opposed the ordinance and cited the unintended consequences listed
  by Ms. Lee as well as the City’s exposure to litigation.

  Mayor PÉREZ suggested that the ordinance include anti-retaliation clauses to further
  protect workers. She addressed Ms. Lee’s concerns regarding store closures in Long
  Beach and explained that the closures were decided before the discussion of the Hero
  Pay ordinance. She went on to discuss the legal decision behind the Long Beach
  ordinance, listed the other cities which had adopted a Hero Pay ordinance, emphasized
  the temporary nature of the pay increase, and agreed with Mr. Montes’s
  recommendations of which models to follow. She sympathized with Ms. Lee’s concerns
  and the opposition of the business community, but stressed the need to support workers
  who were not officially designated hazard employees but were forced to work in
  dangerous environments. She fully supported the ordinance and expressed appreciation
  for the robust conversation.

  Mr. MONTES clarified the process to adopt an urgency ordinance or a regular
  ordinance, the need for a 4/5 vote for an urgency ordinance, as well as the timeline for
  execution for a regular ordinance. Mr. MONTES expanded on Ms. Pérez’s reference of
  anti-retaliatory clauses in the County model and further discussed the other concerns of
  Ms. Lee and Mr. Maza. Ms. LEE continued to express concerns and opposed both an
  urgency and a regular ordinance. Council agreed to move forward with a draft of a
  regular ordinance for first reading at the next Council meeting.

  Action Taken:  City Council directed staff to draft a regular ordinance for first
  reading at the next regular City Council meeting.

CONSENT AGENDA (Item Nos. 9 – 17)

All other items listed under the Consent Agenda were considered by the City Council to be
routine and were enacted by one motion.

9.  2019 STATE HOMELAND SECURITY GRANT – F2M15-25, C2M21-11, M2M21-25

  Staff requested that the City Council approve an agreement with Los Angeles County
  and accept the 2019 State Homeland Security Grant Program (SHSGP). The Los
  Angeles Operational Area (OA) Approval Authority for the Homeland Security Grant
  Program established priorities for approval that focused on enhancing and expanding
  existing specialized resources that would improve the Operational Area’s ability to
  prepare for and respond to terrorism and weapons of mass destruction events, while
  providing an opportunity for cities to apply for funding to meet their needs. The Fire
  Department submitted a grant request in the amount of $74,400 for Urban Search and
  Rescue equipment, supplies and training.

  Discussion:  None.

  Action Taken:  City Council accepted the 2019 State Homeland Security Grant in
  the amount of $74,400 for the Fire Department; authorized the Fire Chief to sign the
  2019 State Homeland Security Grant Program agreement with Los Angeles County,
  subject to final language approval by the City Manager and City Attorney, and to make
  10
3-8-21
   necessary purchases of Urban Search and Rescue equipment, supplies and training as
  submitted to the OA Approval Authority and the State of California Office of Homeland
  Security. (M2M21-25)

  Vote:  Moved:  LEE  Seconded: MALONEY
  Ayes:  MAZA, MALONEY, ANDRADE-STADLER, LEE, PÉREZ
  Noes:  NONE
  Absent: NONE
10.  AUTHORIZE RFP: WATER QUALITY TESTING LABORATORY SERVICES –
  RFP2M21-7, F2M21-29

  The City of Alhambra, as the operator of a community water system, was required by the
  State Water Resources Control Board (SWRCB) to conduct a variety of sampling and
  analytical analyses for drinking water. The City was also required to perform analysis for
  various constituents in accordance with several permits issued by the Los Angeles
  County Sanitation District and Regional Water Quality Control Board. All tests must be
  performed in a certified laboratory which meets State standards. The final one-year
  contract extension of the three additional one-year terms approved in the original
  services contract would expire June 30, 2021. This RFP would provide a one-year
  contract with the option to renew (3) one-year terms if services are satisfactory.

  Public Comment received via email on file in the City Clerk’s office: Yvette
  Cardenas requested that the next staff report include the RFP for public review as well
  as include testing for “forever chemicals.”

  Discussion:  None.

  Action Taken:  City Council approved the distribution of a Request for Proposals
  (RFP) to qualified firms for water quality testing laboratory services with proposals due
  no later than 4:00 p.m. on April 6, 2021; and, directed staff to undertake the steps
  necessary to finalize Council’s action.

  Vote:  Moved:  LEE  Seconded: MALONEY
  Ayes:  MAZA, MALONEY, ANDRADE-STADLER, LEE, PÉREZ
  Noes:  NONE
  Absent:  NONE

11.  AWARD CONTRACT: CONSTRUCTION MANAGEMENT AND INSPECTION
  SERVICES FOR THE VALLEY BOULEVARD SEWER REPLACEMENT PROJECT –
  F2M21-21, RFP2M21-1, C2M21-12, M2M21-26

  On January 11, 2021, the City Council approved the distribution of a Request for
  Proposals for Professional Construction Management and Inspection Services for the
  Valley Boulevard Sewer Replacement Project. There were nine proposals received for
  the project. Staff conducted a review and evaluation of all responding proposals and
  found the Valley Construction Management proposal the best suited for the project.

  Discussion:  None.

  11
3-8-21

15.  RESOLUTION APPROVING THE CLASS SPECIFICATION FOR A GRANTS
  SPECIALIST AND A RESOLUTION ADOPTING A SIDE LETTER OF AGREEMENT
  WITH THE ALHAMBRA CITY EMPLOYEES’ ASSOCIATION – F2M21-2, R2M21-14,
  R2M21-15

  On February 8, 2021, during the City’s Mid-Year Budget Review discussion, the City
  Council directed a grants position be established. The classification of Grants Specialist
  would be created to provide needed grant support to the Management Services
  Department and other City Departments. The position would focus on developing project
  concepts for grant applications, writing proposals, assisting in the implementation of
  projects, monitoring and reporting. The classification of Grant Specialist would be
  supervised by the Management Services Department to ensure alignment with the City’s
  strategic goals. Municipal Code Section 2.48.070 (B) provides that before a class
  specification becomes effective or other changes are made to the City’s Classification
  Plan, it shall first be approved by the City Council. Additionally, the City’s Employer-
  Employee Relations Resolution dictates that “new classifications shall be assigned to an
  employee group as appropriate by the City Manager after advising the affected
  employee organizations.”

  Discussion:  None.

  Action Taken:  City Council, by one motion, took the following actions: 1) Adopted
  Resolution No. R2M21-14 entitled: A Resolution of the Alhambra City Council
  approving the Class Specification for Grants Specialist and approving the City of
  Alhambra Classification Plan; and, 2) Adopted Resolution No. R2M21-15 entitled: A
  Resolution of the Alhambra City Council approving a Side Letter of Agreement with
  Alhambra City Employees’ Association for the inclusion of the Grants Specialist
  classification with the ACEA group and MOU.
